Our work spans 14 countries

Bridges built of light, brick by patient brick.

Bridges of Light Foundation runs cultural-exchange and refugee-resettlement programs across the Mediterranean and East Asia. We were founded in 2009 by a small group of resettlement caseworkers in Geneva. Today we work in fourteen countries, with regional offices in Amman, Tokyo, Beirut, and Berlin.

Donate Volunteer

Lantern Bridge mural, Amman field office, 2024

What we do

Four programs, one practical idea.

Move people across borders with dignity, and move ideas across cultures with care.

All programs
✦

Cultural Exchange

Year-long residencies for writers, translators, and educators between the Mediterranean and East Asia. We move ideas the way we move people — with paperwork, patience, and good hosts on both ends.

Learn more → ◈

Refugee Resettlement

Legal, logistical, and resettlement-after-arrival casework for families fleeing Syria, Sudan, Myanmar, and Afghanistan. We follow families for three years after arrival — not three weeks.

Learn more → ❖

Education Bridges

Language tutoring, credentialing assistance, and university-application support for displaced students. We helped 412 students enroll in 2025.

Learn more → ◉

Emergency Response

A standing fund for the first six weeks after a crisis — when most aid is delayed and most families need cash, papers, and a translator who answers the phone.

Learn more →

More stories
Amman · Jordan

Rana and her grandmother's recipe book

Rana arrived in Amman in 2022 with a tin of saffron, three pairs of shoes, and a handwritten recipe book that had survived the journey from Aleppo in her grandmother's coat pocket. Two years later, she runs a small catering business out of a shared kitchen near the seventh circle, and the recipe book has been copied — by hand — into Arabic, French, and English so her cousins can cook from it too.

«الخبز يحفظ الذاكرة أحسن من الورق.» "Bread holds memory better than paper does." — Rana, quoting her grandmother
Resettlement · arrived September 2022
Tokyo · Japan

Mei, a translator who refused to choose

Mei was born in Kobe, schooled in Geneva, and now runs our Tokyo translation cohort — pairing Japanese poets with Arabic essayists, and watching what survives the crossing. "Translation," she says, "is the slowest form of hospitality." Her cohort published its first bilingual chapbook in March, with editions printed in three scripts.

翻訳ほんやくは、もっとも静しずかな歓待かんたいである。 "Translation is the quietest form of hospitality." — Mei Sato, Tokyo cohort lead
Cultural Exchange · cohort 2025
Berlin · Germany

Yusuf, who finished his thesis on a borrowed laptop

Yusuf left Khartoum in May 2024 with his thesis half-written and his external hard drive in a shoe. He defended in Berlin nine months later, in German — his fourth language. Our Education Bridges program covered translation of his Sudanese transcripts and the rental of the laptop he worked on. He starts his doctorate in October.

"The hardest part was not the language. The hardest part was waking up somewhere where my keyboard was the wrong way around."

Education Bridges · defended February 2025
